proposal.description_short: Executive Order 13769 restricted entry from seven countries; airport detentions prompted emergency court orders, and Trump fired Acting Attorney General Sally Yates.

proposal.description_long: On January 27, 2017, President Donald Trump signed Executive Order 13769, which suspended refugee admissions and restricted entry for 90 days for nationals of seven predominantly Muslim countries. The order took effect amid reports of detentions at U.S. airports. The Associated Press reported that a federal judge issued an emergency order temporarily barring deportation of travelers covered by the ban, while the American Civil Liberties Union described specific travelers detained at Logan Airport. Acting Attorney General Sally Yates then instructed Justice Department attorneys not to present arguments defending the order because she was not convinced it was lawful. proposal.title: 2019 U.S.–Honduras Asylum Agreement Set a Framework for Third-Country Transfers
proposal.description_short: The 2019 U.S.–Honduras agreement allowed certain asylum seekers to be transferred to Honduras, subject to exceptions.
proposal.description_medium: The United States and Honduras signed an Asylum Cooperative Agreement on September 25, 2019. Its text provided for transferring certain non-Honduran nationals who arrived at or between U.S. ports of entry and requested protection to pursue claims in Honduras. It excluded Honduran nationals, unaccompanied minors, and specified visa holders or travelers who did not need a Honduran visa. The agreement entered into force on March 25, 2020; the agreement alone does not establish how many transfers occurred or the protections available in practice.
proposal.description_long: The United States and Honduras signed an Asylum Cooperative Agreement on September 25, 2019, establishing a framework under which some people seeking protection after arriving at or between U.S. ports of entry could be transferred to Honduras to pursue protection there. The agreement did not cover everyone: it excluded Honduran nationals and unaccompanied children, and it provided exceptions for certain people with valid U.S. visas or who were not required to obtain a visa to enter Honduras. The agreement entered into force on March 25, 2020. It called for the governments to develop operating procedures and an implementation plan addressing transfers and the receiving system’s capacity. The Department of Homeland Security described the arrangement as a route for third-country nationals, rather than a rule automatically sending every asylum seeker to Honduras. The text establishes the agreement’s scope and formal mechanism, but it does not establish how many people were transferred, whether each person obtained access to a fair asylum process, or how protections operated in practice. This draft describes the agreement and its limits without claiming that asylum protection was eliminated.

proposal.title: Trump Pardoned Joseph Arpaio After Criminal-Contempt Finding
proposal.description_short: A federal judge found Joe Arpaio guilty of criminal contempt for willfully violating a court order; Trump pardoned him before sentencing in August 2017.
proposal.description_medium: On July 31, 2017, a federal judge found former Maricopa County sheriff Joe Arpaio guilty of criminal contempt for willfully violating a court order in the Melendres immigration-enforcement case. Before sentencing, President Donald Trump pardoned him on August 25, 2017. DOJ’s clemency list records contempt of court and no sentence. The record supports the finding and pardon, not a corrupt motive.
proposal.description_long: On July 31, 2017, U.S. District Judge Susan Bolton found former Maricopa County sheriff Joe Arpaio guilty of criminal contempt after a five-day bench trial. The court found that Arpaio willfully violated a federal order in Melendres v. Arpaio restricting the sheriff’s office from detaining people based solely on suspected unlawful presence in the United States. President Donald Trump granted Arpaio a full pardon on August 25, 2017, before sentencing. The Justice Department’s clemency list records the offense as contempt of court and lists no sentence. In a later order, the district court explained that the pardon spared Arpaio from punishment but did not revise the historical facts of the case. These records support a factual account of the contempt finding and pardon. They do not establish that Trump issued the pardon in exchange for political loyalty or that the clemency was corrupt, so the original “Corrupt Pardons” subcategory is removed.
